SOURCE: "Billion-scale similarity search with GPUs", Jeff Johnson, Matthijs Douze, Hervé Jégou (Facebook AI Research). The PDF file is arXiv 1702.08734v1 [cs.CV], dated 28 Feb 2017. It is not the IEEE Trans. Big Data 2021 version. The filename says 2019. Cite it as the arXiv v1 text, or check that the journal version has the same numbers.

COVERAGE: I read all 65,938 of 65,938 characters across pages 1–12. That covers the body, Sections 1–7, the references and the Appendix (the WarpSelect complexity derivation). I skipped nothing. I skimmed the references only for where methods come from.

CLAIMS
- claim: IVFADC is a two-level quantization. A coarse quantizer q1 assigns each vector to one inverted list, and a fine product quantizer q2 encodes the residual. At search time, only the τ lists closest to the query are scanned.
  number: none
  setup: the indexing structure used throughout the paper (from Jégou et al. 2011)
  quote: "y≈q(y) =q1(y) +q2(y−q1(y))" ... "The multi-probe parameter τ is the number of coarse-level centroids we consider." ... "boils down to linearly scanning τ inverted lists."
  where: p2, about chars 7,500–9,500
- claim: Rule of thumb for list count: the number of coarse centroids is about the square root of the database size, trained with k-means. PQ codes shorter than the stored ID make no sense.
  number: |C1|≈√ℓ; ID 4 or 8 bytes
  setup: general design guidance
  quote: "We typically use |C1|≈ √𝓁, trained via k-means." / "The ID of the vector (a 4- or 8-byte integer) is also stored in the inverted lists, so it makes no sense to have shorter codes than that"
  where: p2
- claim: A product quantizer splits a vector into b sub-vectors, each quantized to one of 256 centroids. The result is a b-byte code with 256^b reproduction values.
  number: 256 per sub-quantizer; b bytes
  setup: general
  quote: "The sub-quantizers typically have 256 reproduction values, to fit in one byte." ... "the product quantizer generates b-byte codes with |C2| = 256 b reproduction values."
  where: p2–3. The extraction drops the superscript, so "256 b" means 256^b.
- claim: PQ is fast because of lookup tables. You precompute 256 distances per sub-quantizer, and each database distance then becomes b lookups and adds instead of d multiply-adds.
  number: 256×d multiply-adds + n×b lookup-adds vs n×d
  setup: per query, per inverted list
  quote: "Explicit computation: n×d mutiply-adds; • With lookup tables: 256 ×d multiply-adds and n×b lookup-adds. This is the key to the efficiency of the product quantizer."
  where: p6, Section 5.2
- claim: Speed/recall on SIFT1M: at the same time budget as the prior GPU method, FAISS gets much higher recall.
  number: R@1 0.80 vs 0.51; R@100 0.95 vs 0.86; 0.02 ms/query
  setup: SIFT1M, Titan X, compared with Wieschollek et al. 2016
  quote: "They obtain a nearest neighbor recall at 1 (fraction of queries where the true nearest neighbor is in the top 1 result) of R@1 = 0.51, and R@100 = 0.86 in 0.02 ms per query on a Titan X. For the same time budget, our implementation obtains R@1 = 0.80 and R@100 = 0.95."
  where: p9, Section 6.4
- claim: At billion scale with 8-byte codes, it is slightly more accurate and 8.5× faster than the prior GPU state of the art.
  number: R@10 0.376 at 17.7 µs vs 0.35 at 150 µs; 8.5×
  setup: SIFT1B, nq=10^4, one GPU, m=8 bytes/vector, matched memory
  quote: "On a single GPU, with m = 8 bytes per vector, R@10 = 0.376 in 17.7µs per query vector, versus their reported R@10 = 0.35 in 150 µs per query vector. Thus, our implementation is more accurate at a speed 8.5× faster."
  where: p9
- claim: On Deep1B, OPQ plus IVFPQ sharded across 4 GPUs matches a CPU baseline's recall about 1,500× faster per query. The hardware differs.
  number: R@1 0.4517 in 0.0133 ms vs 0.45 in 20 ms; 20 GB
  setup: Deep1B, m=20, d=80 via OPQ, |C1|=2^18, 4 GPUs S=2 R=2; baseline is a 1-thread CPU
  quote: "R@1 = 0.45 in 20 ms search time per vector. We use a PQ encoding of m = 20, with d = 80 via OPQ [17], and|C1| = 218, which uses a comparable dataset storage as the original paper (20 GB)." ... "We obtain a R@1 = 0.4517 in 0.0133 ms per vector. While the hardware platforms are different"
  where: p9. "218" is 2^18, flattened in extraction.
- claim: τ (nprobe) is the speed/quality knob. The authors sweep it from 1 to 256 for each code size.
  number: τ 1–256; m = 16/32/64 (YFCC), 20/40 (Deep1B)
  setup: k-NN graph construction, YFCC100M 95M images at d=128, |C1|=2^16; Deep1B with OPQ to d=120, |C1|=2^18
  quote: "For a given encoding, we vary τ from 1 to 256, to obtain trade-offs between efficiency and quality, as seen in Figure 5."
  where: p9
- claim: End-to-end k-NN graph build times.
  number: >0.8 accuracy in 35 min (95M); 6 h low quality / about half a day high quality (1B)
  setup: 10-NN, 4 Titan X (YFCC S=1 R=4); time includes indexing
  quote: "An accuracy of more than 0.8 is obtained in 35 minutes. For Deep1B, a lower-quality graph can be built in 6 hours, with higher quality in about half a day."
  where: p10
- claim: Adding GPUs gives less than linear speedup.
  number: ~1.6× (m=20), ~1.7× (m=40) going from 4 to 8 GPUs
  setup: Deep1B, 8 M40s
  quote: "Performance is improved sub-linearly (∼ 1.6× for m = 20,∼ 1.7× for m = 40)."
  where: p10
- claim: Replication splits queries across GPUs. Sharding splits the database across GPUs and needs an extra k-selection merge, so it is usually slower than replication.
  number: none
  setup: multi-GPU
  quote: "sharding will yield a speedup ... but is usually less than pure replication due to fixed overhead and cost of subsequent k-selection."
  where: p7, Section 5.4
- claim: k-selection (WarpSelect) is the core contribution. It reaches 55% of peak memory bandwidth at k=100 but only 16% at k=1000.
  number: 55% / 16%; 1.62× and 2.01× vs fgknn
  setup: one Titan X, nq=10000, ℓ=128000, random floats
  quote: "W arpSelectis 1.62× faster atk = 100, 2.01× atk = 1000." / "W arpSelectoperates at 55% of peak at k = 100 but only 16% of peak at k = 1000."
  where: p8
- claim: Exact brute-force search is a GEMM followed by a fused k-select. Fusing matters.
  number: 85% of peak; ≥25% slower unfused; full sort >10× slower
  setup: SIFT1M exact, 1 Titan X
  quote: "our method, which has 85 % of the peak possible performance" / "Our same exact algorithm without fusion (requiring an additional pass through D′) is at least 25% slower."
  where: p8–9
- claim: Exact GPU k-means is more than 2× faster than BIDMach and close to linear across 4 GPUs.
  number: 140 s vs 320 s (256 centroids); 316 s vs 735 s (4096); 3.16× on 4 GPUs
  setup: MNIST8m, 8.1M×784-d, 20 iterations
  quote: "Ours 1 140 s 316 s" / "(3.16× for 4 GPUs with 4096 centroids)"
  where: p8, Table 1
- claim: The shared-memory lookup tables cap the number of PQ sub-quantizers.
  number: b ≤ 48 (fp32) or 96 (fp16); b a multiple of 4 up to 64
  setup: GPU architectures of the time
  quote: "This limits b to at most 48 (32-bit floating point) or 96 (16-bit floating point) with current architectures."
  where: p6

LIMITS
- The paper is about GPUs and IVFADC only. It covers no graph indexes (HNSW is never mentioned), no LSH or binary-code baselines beyond prose dismissal, and no filtering, deletes or updates.
- The authors say IMI, LOPQ and polysemous codes are "too complex to be implemented efficiently on GPUs". OPQ is used only as preprocessing.
- The Deep1B comparison is GPU against 1-thread CPU: "While the hardware platforms are different".
- The k-means benchmark is "somewhat unrealistic, as one would typically sub-sample".
- WarpSelect falls to 16% of peak at large k. The fused IVF kernel helped "at most 15%" and was not adopted.
- There is no full recall-vs-nprobe table. Figure 5 is a curve that the extraction does not preserve.
- What has dated: Maxwell Titan X, CUDA 8.0, register and shared-memory limits from 2017, and k ≤ 1024.

BUILDS ON: Jégou, Douze, Schmid 2011, product quantization / IVFADC [25]. Ge et al. 2014, OPQ [17]. Babenko & Lempitsky 2012, inverted multi-index [4]; 2014, bilayer PQ / table decomposition [5]; 2016, Deep1B [6]. Jégou et al. 2011, SIFT1B [26]. Batcher 1968, bitonic sorting [8]. Tang et al. 2015, fgknn merge queue [41]. Wieschollek et al. 2016, prior GPU ANN [47]. André et al. 2015, PQ fast scan [2]. Dong et al. 2011, NN-Descent [15].

CODE: none. There are only pseudocode algorithms. Algorithm 4 "IVFPQ batch search routine" (p7) is the most useful for "FAISS by hand": coarse τ-argmin, then per-list distance tables, then lookup-sum, then k-select.

FIGURES
- Fig 5, p9: speed/accuracy trade-off of 10-NN graph construction for YFCC100M and DEEP1B. Shows recall against time as τ and code size vary, which explains the nprobe trade-off faster than prose. Axis text did not extract.
- Fig 3, p8: k-selection runtimes against array length, compared with peak bandwidth.
- Fig 4, p9: exact SIFT1M k-NN time against k, split into GEMM and k-select cost.
- Figs 1, 2 (p4–5): sorting network and WarpSelect structure. These are GPU internals and of low value for the note.

PROBLEMS
- The file is arXiv v1 from 2017, not the 2019/2021 version named in the brief.
- Extraction flattens superscripts: "218" is 2^18, "216" is 2^16, "256 b" is 256^b, "106/104" is 10^6/10^4.
- All axis labels and data in Figures 3–5 came out as garbled glyphs, so I quoted no numbers from the plots.
- There were no embedded instructions.
